section_summary: This section documents U.S. monitoring of Japanese purchases of scrap iron and steel, nitrate, aviation gasoline, military equipment, and other strategic materials during 1933–1934. It includes official correspondence over Panama Canal scrap and Shipping Board vessels, consular reports and citizen tips about Japanese buying activity across the Americas, and cross-references to related intelligence. A substantial group of British press clippings covers the arms embargo, Manchuria, Yōsuke Matsuoka’s diplomacy, anti-war efforts to stop scrap shipments, and wider commercial and strategic concerns about Japan.

subfiles.title: Justice Department transmittal of complaint concerning Sun Shipbuilding scrap shipments
subfiles.from: Roy St. Lewis, Assistant Attorney General
subfiles.about: Transmits an anonymous worker’s letter and a newspaper clipping about former government ships and scrap allegedly being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department of Justice forwards material concerning Sun Shipbuilding Company’s breaking up of former government vessels and shipment of their scrap to Japan. The enclosures are an unsigned March 24 letter from Chester and a related press clipping.

subfiles.title: Japan Buys Arms
subfiles.about: Reports that two former Canadian steamers might load munitions in Britain for Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: The clipping says the Canadian Mariner and Canadian Inventor had been sold to the Sun Shipping Company. It reports that Japanese interests were expected to obtain the ships and that both might load munitions at Bristol.

subfiles.title: Anonymous Sun Shipbuilding employee’s warning about scrap exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Alleges that Sun companies were scrapping former government ships and selling scrap and oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The writer says ships obtained from the government and associated with Hog Island were being cut up at Chester and their scrap sent to Japan. He asks whether the Sun Shipping Company mentioned in the enclosed clipping is connected with his employer and asserts that the related Sun Oil Company had long sold oil to Japan. He presents the activity as dangerous because he expects a future U.S.-Japanese war.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the legality and policy of a proposed scrap sale
subfiles.about: Concludes that law and treaty pose no objection to a proposed transaction and advises against departmental disapproval.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum finds no legal or treaty obstacle to the contemplated sale. It nevertheless treats the policy question separately and doubts that the Department should express disapproval.

subfiles.title: Proposed Sale of Iron and Steel Scrap by the Panama Canal Administration
subfiles.about: Requests views on whether Panama Canal scrap sought by Japanese interests might be used for munitions.
subfiles.summary: Wilson forwards a copy of the Chief Quartermaster’s letter supplied by Mr. Smith of the Panama Canal Legal Adviser’s Office. He notes that a Japanese purchase might be harmless but could conceivably supply munitions and asks whether relevant information is available.

subfiles.title: Panama Canal request to advertise 8,324 tons of iron and steel scrap
subfiles.about: Lists surplus scrap, reports Japanese interest, and asks for both policy advice and an invitation for bids.
subfiles.summary: Watson inventories approximately 8,324 net tons of iron and steel scrap held in the Canal Zone. Local intermediaries had made tentative offers for Japanese interests, although officials did not know whether the ultimate buyer was governmental or commercial. Because storage was overcrowded, Watson requests prompt advertising while retaining the right to reject bids.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Panama Canal scrap-sale request
subfiles.about: Duplicates the request to advertise the Canal Zone’s accumulation of iron and steel scrap.
subfiles.summary: This duplicate repeats the inventory of roughly 8,324 tons and the report of tentative Japanese offers. It cites the explanation that Japanese scrap imports served earthquake-resistant construction and asks that bids be solicited despite unresolved policy concerns.

subfiles.title: State Department reply declining to opine on the Panama Canal scrap sale
subfiles.to: A. L. Flint, Chief, Panama Canal Office
subfiles.about: Returns the Quartermaster’s letter and states that the Department does not wish to express an opinion on the proposed sale.
subfiles.summary: Wilson returns the Panama Canal correspondence supplied through Mr. Smith. After consideration, the State Department declines to take a position on whether the iron and steel scrap should be sold.

subfiles.title: Enclosed clean copy of the Panama Canal scrap-sale request
subfiles.about: Provides the clean copy of Watson’s request that accompanied the State Department’s reply.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure lists the Canal Zone’s 8,324 tons of scrap and describes tentative approaches by local representatives of Japanese interests. Watson asks for an opinion but also urges immediate advertising because storage facilities are crowded.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Paris report on Russian military supplies for Japan
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to file 861.60/271 for a Paris report on Russian manufacture of military supplies for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The file note contains no substantive report. It points to another decimal-file location concerning military supplies manufactured by Russia for Japan.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs routing memorandum on a commercial inquiry
subfiles.about: Routes a commercial inquiry and attaches a 1932 statement of policy on sales of iron and steel scrap.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs considers the attached letter a commercial inquiry falling under Murphy’s jurisdiction, a view in which Eastern European Affairs concurs. For background, it supplies the Department’s March 25, 1932 letter to the Navy outlining scrap-sale policy.

subfiles.title: Eastern European Affairs telephone-conversation note
subfiles.from: L. W. H., Division of Eastern European Affairs
subfiles.about: Records that the matter had already been discussed with Dooman by telephone.
subfiles.summary: This brief routing note refers the subject to Far Eastern Affairs and Mr. Dooman. The writer states only that the matter had been discussed by telephone.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about buyers and sellers of Japanese and Russian scrap steel
subfiles.about: Requests information identifying firms buying and selling scrap steel for Japan and Russia.
subfiles.summary: Ernst says the Seattle Chamber of Commerce advised him to approach the State Department. He asks who purchases scrap steel for the Japanese and Russian governments and who supplies each country.

subfiles.title: Commercial Office referral of Ernst’s scrap-steel inquiry
subfiles.to: Iron and Steel Division, Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.about: Forwards Ernst’s inquiry for action and a direct reply.
subfiles.summary: The Commercial Office transmits a copy of Ernst’s August 26 letter to the appropriate commerce bureau. It notes that Ernst has been informed of the referral.
keywords: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce

subfiles.title: Reply notifying Ernst of the Commerce Bureau referral
subfiles.from: James J. Murphy Jr., Chief, Commercial Office
subfiles.about: Advises Ernst that his inquiry has been referred to the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce.
subfiles.summary: Murphy explains that the Commerce Bureau is legally responsible for disseminating commercial information. Ernst’s request concerning Japanese and Russian government scrap buyers has therefore been sent there for direct handling.

subfiles.title: Changes to digest of Japanese public donations for army and navy equipment
subfiles.from: R. S. Bratton, Acting Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Updates a digest table of equipment financed by Japanese public donations.
subfiles.summary: The report states the total amount of public donations for army and navy equipment and supplies revised quantities for aircraft, antiaircraft weapons, machine guns, tanks, vehicles, communications equipment, helmets, gas masks, and ammunition. It cites a War Office press release as its source.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Colombo report on Japanese purchases of scrap, ore, and plumbago
subfiles.about: Points to a report showing a sharp increase in Japanese purchases of scrap iron, ore, and plumbago.
subfiles.summary: The note says Japanese purchases during the first ten months of 1933 exceeded the comparable 1931 level by more than three times. They were also nearly double the 1932 figure despite reduced Japanese military operations in 1933.

subfiles.title: Illegible citizen letter seeking investigation of material reportedly destined for Japan
subfiles.about: Urges official attention to a poorly legible report involving industrial materials or weapons and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The handwriting and OCR are too damaged for a reliable full transcription, but the correspondent asks that the President or federal departments examine the matter. The surviving text appears to refer to guns or industrial material connected with Japan and offers further help or information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Chilean nitrate negotiations
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a telegram on Japanese negotiations for 20,000 tons of Chilean nitrate for military use.
subfiles.summary: The file note supplies the related telegram and decimal-file references. Its subject is a confidential Japanese-Chilean nitrate negotiation believed to have military purposes.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting Japanese negotiations for Chilean nitrate
subfiles.about: Reports confidential negotiations for Japan to buy 20,000 tons of Chilean nitrate, presumably for military purposes.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy learned from a source it regarded as direct and unimpeachable that the Japanese government was negotiating with Chile’s finance minister. The unusual avoidance of the Nitrate Sales Corporation suggested a military purpose, although the transaction had not yet closed.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on worldwide Japanese purchases of metal junk
subfiles.about: Notes numerous reports of Japanese metal-junk buying and questions the relative usefulness of scrap and ore.
subfiles.summary: The writer says reports of Japanese purchases of metal junk had arrived from many parts of the world. Referring to an earlier shipment from Atlanta, the memorandum recalls an argument that old iron and steel could be used more profitably than ore or pig iron, while disclaiming technical expertise.

subfiles.title: Purchases of Junk by Japanese Government
subfiles.about: Reports A. Sendel’s purchases of Venezuelan metal junk under an asserted Japanese government contract.
subfiles.summary: Summerlin reports that Sendel of West Indies Iron and Metal Exporters was buying large quantities of junk in Caracas and loading chartered vessels at Trinidad for Japan. Sendel claimed his firm held a Japanese government contract, with 75 percent of cargo value payable against bills of lading and the remainder after inspection in Japan. The despatch places the buying within a broader pattern of Japanese shipping, commercial, and oil activity in Venezuela.

subfiles.title: Bradford letter concerning railroad scrap allegedly routed to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the dismantling of old railroad cars and locomotives and an indirect shipment route allegedly ending in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bradford says a company was burning hundreds of Southern Railroad boxcars and cutting up 85 old engines. He had been told the scrap went first to Pennsylvania and then through San Francisco to Japan, a routing he considered suspicious. He offers further information if the trade is improper.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese purchase of aviation gasoline for Manchuria
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, American Consul General at Nanking
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese government order for 2.7 million gallons of aviation gasoline for prompt delivery in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Peck says the Socony-Vacuum Oil Company supplied the information confidentially. The reported buyer was the Japanese government and the destination was Manchuria; the message was repeated to the Legation.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Nanking aviation-gasoline telegram
subfiles.about: Paraphrases Peck’s report of the Japanese aviation-gasoline order.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase states that Socony-Vacuum confidentially informed the American Consul General at Nanking of the purchase. It gives the amount as 2.7 million gallons and says delivery in Manchuria was expected shortly.

subfiles.title: Archives-retention routing note
subfiles.about: Asks whether Far Eastern Affairs wishes to retain the preceding material in its archives.
subfiles.summary: This is a brief administrative routing slip. It asks Far Eastern Affairs to decide whether the information should be kept in archival files.

subfiles.title: Summary of British press comments, March 6–8, 1933
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes nine British press items concerning China, Japan, Manchuria, arms, railways, and alleged Japanese air bases.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews parliamentary discussion of China’s League contributions and an Anti-War League attempt to halt a scrap cargo for Japan. It summarizes commentary on Manchukuo, the arms embargo, Wellington Koo’s appeal for support, and planned railways linking Manchuria to Rashin. It dismisses as alarmist a report alleging that Matsuoka sought Dutch concessions for disguised Japanese air bases.

subfiles.title: Schedule of British press comments transmitted from London
subfiles.about: Lists nine transmitted British press items dated March 6–8.
subfiles.summary: The schedule identifies the newspaper and general subject of each enclosure. Subjects include China’s League contributions, munitions, scrap iron, Manchukuo, the arms embargo, railways, and alleged jungle air bases.

subfiles.title: League of Nations Contributions (China)
subfiles.about: Records questions concerning China’s arrears in contributions to the League of Nations.
subfiles.summary: Sir John Simon explains the installment arrangement for China’s 1922–1930 arrears and identifies unpaid portions of the 1931 and 1932 assessments. Members question which Chinese government owes the money and whether states in arrears should retain League privileges.

subfiles.title: China and Japan (Munitions)
subfiles.about: Records parliamentary debate over an international arms embargo and protection of British interests during the fighting in China.
subfiles.summary: Members press the government about foreign participation in an embargo on arms exports to China and Japan. Sir John Simon says there is no universal agreement and indicates the issue will be raised at Geneva. The debate also covers threats to British interests in Jehol and North China, licensing of arms exports, and overseas factories owned by British firms.

subfiles.title: Scrap Iron Cargo for Japan: Attempt to Persuade Crew Not to Sail
subfiles.about: Reports an Anti-War League effort to prevent the Stanleyville carrying scrap metal from Blyth to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Anti-war activists argued that the cargo would become munitions for use against China and tried to persuade the crew not to sail. A British Anti-War Council meeting raised money for the crew if they refused, but delegates arrived at Blyth only after the vessel had departed.

subfiles.title: Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Argues for recognition of Manchukuo and criticizes the League and Britain’s arms-embargo policy.
subfiles.summary: The editorial predicts that Japan will consolidate Manchukuo and suppress remaining resistance. It portrays League nonrecognition and British idealism as futile and contends that recognizing Manchukuo would allow Britain to share in its prospective trade.

subfiles.title: The Embargo
subfiles.about: Criticizes Britain’s likely retreat from its arms embargo on both Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: The editorial argues that only an international prohibition directed against Japan would accord with the League’s finding of aggression. It says Britain’s provisional bilateral embargo alienated both sides and that reversing it would damage British credibility.

subfiles.title: China’s Case Against Japan
subfiles.from: V. K. Wellington Koo, News Chronicle
subfiles.about: Presents China’s argument for moral, diplomatic, and economic support against Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Koo describes Japan’s operations in Manchuria and Jehol as part of a wider program of conquest and warns that inaction will undermine collective security and disarmament. He argues that China does not seek foreign troops but expects treaty partners to provide moral, diplomatic, and economic support while withholding assistance from Japan. He urges concerted action to restore respect for international law.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Secret Jungle Air Bases
subfiles.about: Alleges that Japanese concessions in Borneo and New Guinea were intended to create disguised air bases on a route toward Australia.
subfiles.summary: The article claims Dutch aviators found levelled spaces resembling aerodromes within Japanese rubber concessions in Borneo. It links these suspicions to Matsuoka’s reported interest in Dutch New Guinea and an alleged nonaggression proposal to Holland. A related item announces a planned BBC discussion involving Chinese minister Quo Tai-chi.

subfiles.title: Schedule of British press comments transmitted March 21, 1933
subfiles.about: Lists thirteen press and parliamentary items concerning Japan, China, the arms embargo, trade, and Matsuoka.
subfiles.summary: The cover sheet inventories British articles and debates from March 7–20. Subjects include the lifting of the embargo, Japanese diplomacy, a Brazilian warship proposal, scrap shipments, Japanese imports, and Matsuoka’s War Office visit.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Search for Allies
subfiles.about: Reports Matsuoka’s appeal for renewed cooperation among Britain, the United States, and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Matsuoka tells British and American journalists that the end of the Anglo-Japanese alliance created a destabilizing vacuum in the Far East. He rejects the Lytton Commission’s view of Manchuria and also comments on Russia’s future development.

subfiles.title: Coffee in Exchange for Warships
subfiles.about: Reports a Brazilian proposal to barter coffee and other products for Japanese-built warships.
subfiles.summary: Brazil was reportedly seeking information on construction of thirty cruisers, destroyers, and service vessels. Payment would be made through Brazilian commodities over twelve years, and British firms had also been approached.

subfiles.title: Attempt to Stop Ship Sailing for Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the prosecution of a docker who entered shipyard premises while trying to stop a scrap-metal vessel sailing for Japan.
subfiles.summary: John Davison said he wanted to board the Stanleyville, meet its crew, and persuade them not to carry what he regarded as war material to Japan. Police had guarded the premises because trouble was expected, and Davison was remanded on bail.

subfiles.title: Mr. Matsuoka’s Tour
subfiles.from: The Times correspondent at The Hague
subfiles.about: Describes Matsuoka’s European itinerary and his interest in Japanese settlement in Dutch New Guinea.
subfiles.summary: After two days in The Hague, Matsuoka planned to visit Brussels, Paris, and London. He expressed interest in Japanese emigration to Dutch New Guinea and spoke favorably of a possible Dutch-Japanese nonaggression agreement before meeting Paul Hymans.

subfiles.title: Japanese Imports and British Trade
subfiles.about: Provides statistics and parliamentary questions on Japanese exports to the British Empire and competition with British industry.
subfiles.summary: The debate gives figures for British aircraft exports and for Japanese merchandise sold throughout the British Empire in 1932. Members question the government about Japanese competition, especially in pottery, and discuss possible protective measures. The table identifies British India as the largest listed imperial market for Japanese exports.

subfiles.title: Mr. Matsuoka at the War Office
subfiles.about: Reports Matsuoka’s meetings with British industrial, military, and business figures in London.
subfiles.summary: Matsuoka visited Imperial Chemical Industries and met its chairman, Sir Harry McGowan. Accompanied by Yoshizawa, he then spoke with Lord Hailsham at the War Office, dined with City businessmen, and attended the Japanese Club before departing for New York.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Swedish munitions report
subfiles.about: Points to a report that Swedish manufacturers were declining further munitions orders attributed indirectly to the Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: The note says the purchases were made through intermediaries. An informant nevertheless identified the Japanese government as the actual buyer and reported that additional manufacturing orders were being refused.

subfiles.title: Justice Department report of scrap sales from Wilmington to Japan
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Division of Investigation
subfiles.about: Forwards a North Carolina deputy sheriff’s report that local junk dealers sold scrap iron to the Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: Hoover reports that A. A. McAdams had learned of ten or fifteen carloads of scrap iron sold by two Wilmington junk dealers. He forwards the information for possible interest and says it was also supplied to the Office of Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Metal Purchases at Curaçao and other Caribbean ports
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese steamer collecting scrap metal purchased by A. Sendel across the Caribbean.
subfiles.summary: Brooks reports that the vessel loaded between 1,500 and 1,600 tons at Curaçao after taking scrap at Puerto Rico, Trinidad, and Demerara. The buyer was West Indies Iron and Metal Exporters, represented by A. Sendel. Sendel also claimed to have arranged a June shipment of 3,000 tons from the Lago company in Aruba to Japan.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser memorandum on termination of the Boston Iron and Metal contract
subfiles.about: Explains the Shipping Board’s cancellation of a vessel-scrapping contract whose output was reportedly destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says Mr. O’Hara reported that scrap from Shipping Board vessels had been bought by the Japanese government and was being exported as quickly as the ships could be broken up. Following Cabinet discussion, further vessels were withheld. To avoid implying that Japan itself constituted a declared emergency, the Legal Adviser recommended emphasizing the Attorney General’s conclusion that the contract was unauthorized and illegal.

subfiles.title: Contract of the Boston Iron & Metal Co., Senate Document No. 177
subfiles.from: Daniel C. Roper, Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.about: Responds to a Senate resolution concerning withdrawal and invalidation of a contract to scrap government merchant vessels.
subfiles.summary: Roper explains that undelivered vessels were withdrawn because they might be needed for U.S. commerce and because the contract permitted retention for operation. He cites the Attorney General’s opinion that vessels with operating values far above scrap value could not lawfully be sold for scrapping, contrasting an $11.47 million operating valuation with a proposed scrap return of roughly $558,000. The document also reports that 169 of 277 government vessels were recommended for retention as naval auxiliaries and begins reproducing the Attorney General’s April 19 opinion.
